title: No Measurable Benefit from Verifier‑Assisted Generate→Validate→Repair under Shared‑Initial Generation: A Preregistered Emulation Study
abstract: We preregistered and autonomously executed a paired emulation study (study‑cnd‑2026‑001) to test whether a verifier‑assisted generate→validate→repair pipeline increases oracle pass rates for LLM‑produced network configurations on vendor‑diverse emulated NetOps intent→configuration tasks. The frozen design used shared_initial_candidate generation semantics (one generator call per pair consumed by both conditions), declared model gpt‑5‑mini, a deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5), and a repair budget ≤1 call/task. Execution produced 200 complete pairs (400 episodes), model_calls_used=200, and repair_calls_invoked=0. Results: baseline = 200/200 oracle passes; guarded = 200/200 oracle passes; absolute paired difference = 0.00 (paired bootstrap 95% CI [0.00, 0.00], bootstrap_resamples=10000, seed=1729); McNemar two‑sided p = 1.00. The null result is design‑bound: every shared candidate passed the deterministic oracle, so the repair stage was never exercised. We release the full audited artifact bundle (preregistration, prompts, raw outputs, provider traces, validator traces, execution manifest and SHA‑256 digests) and provide artifact‑anchored recommendations for informative follow‑ups (independent generation semantics, calibrated difficulty, larger repair budgets, validator stress tests).

sections.introduction:
Generative LLMs are being proposed as intent→configuration agents for NetOps because they can map human intent to device configurations with little manual encoding. Operational adoption requires reliably correct outputs (ordering, vendor idiom, transient‑state safety). A common mitigation architecture is generate→validate→repair: the LLM proposes a candidate; a deterministic validator (oracle) checks objective safety and correctness predicates; failing artifacts trigger generator‑guided repair. Prior work has reported improvements when validators constrain generation or when repairs use verifier counterexamples, but reproducible, preregistered, artifact‑anchored measurements of repair benefit remain limited.

We designed study‑cnd‑2026‑001 to produce a confirmatory, auditable measurement of whether verifier assistance increases oracle pass rates in an emulated NetOps environment. The preregistration froze the estimand, task bank, generation semantics (shared_initial_candidate), model (gpt‑5‑mini), validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5), repair budget (≤1), and analysis executor (paired_binary_analysis_v1). All artifacts (prompts, raw outputs, provider traces, validator traces, manifests) were archived with SHA‑256 digests for deterministic reconciliation. The research question we test is: Does an automated verifier‑assisted generate→validate→repair pipeline significantly increase the oracle pass rate (reduce misconfiguration) relative to unconstrained LLM generation across vendor‑diverse emulated NetOps intent→configuration tasks under the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics?
sections.related_work: Relevant prior work spans constraint‑guided LLM adaptation, intent→configuration synthesis, and verifier‑grounded repair loops. Representative studies that motivated the design include MeshAgent (constraint‑guided generation for NetOps), NetConfEval (intent→configuration benchmarking), and verifier‑grounded program repair workflows (StruSpec), each emphasizing verifier roles in operational correctness. Those works and broader surveys of LLM evaluation and verifier‑augmented repair informed our preregistration decisions (see cited_record_ids). Unlike many prior contributions, we preregistered the experimental estimand and generation semantics, executed the run autonomously, and archived per‑file hashes and deterministic reconciliation artifacts so every principal number reported below can be traced to a stored file.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration: The experiment was preregistered as study‑cnd‑2026‑001 (preregistration SHA‑256 a8969ac01f3b1bb7585872c58a92f72d0752160dd4e6e01cbafbfe0d15073ad2). The preregistration froze the primary_estimand (paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline), sample size (Npairs=200), stratification (protocol buckets BGP/OSPF/ACL/VLAN = 50 each; per‑protocol vendor allocation Cisco=17, Juniper=17, Arista=16), generation semantics (shared_initial_candidate), model (gpt‑5‑mini), validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5), repair budget (≤1 repair call/task), and analysis plan (paired bootstrap percentile CI with 10,000 resamples, seed=1729, plus exact McNemar two‑sided test). The full preregistration artifact is archived and hashed in the execution bundle.

Task bank and emulation: The task manifest (execution/task_manifest.jsonl) lists 200 paired tasks. Each task entry includes: human intent text, initial network state, expected final state, required_sequence of operations, constraints, and a canonical reference_answer. Representative tasks and their scoring records are archived (e.g., execution/scoring/task-000001-baseline.json; SHA‑256 eaf96aec12c30860...). Tasks were synthesized to span common NetOps operations (MTU/VLAN changes, uplink failover, controlled shutdown‑modify‑restore sequences) and two complexity levels (simple/complex). The emulated network model and deterministic validator implement interpretable predicates (reachability, protected interface preservation, required sequence enforcement); validator traces include parsed_command_count, normalized_configuration, final_state dictionaries, and a valid boolean.

Generation semantics, model and adapter: The frozen generation semantics were shared_initial_candidate (one generator call per pair; the produced candidate was supplied verbatim to both baseline and guarded scorers). The declared generator was gpt‑5‑mini via adapter family hosted_netops_gvr_v1; the model configuration artifact is execution/model_configuration.json (SHA‑256 1acce92558edeb13...). All provider call traces are archived under execution/provider_calls/ and hashed.

Validator, repair and scoring: The deterministic_netops_validator_v5 scored each candidate and returned a structured validation trace (validation_before and validation_after, violation lists, and normalized_configuration). Repair was permitted by design but in this run was never invoked (repair_applied=false in every validator trace). The scoring rule for the primary estimand was a binary oracle pass/fail (score: 1 = valid configuration meeting constraints and required sequence; 0 = invalid). All scoring JSONs are archived under execution/scoring/ with per‑file hashes.

Statistical analysis: The preregistered analysis executor paired_binary_analysis_v1 computed the paired estimate (guarded − baseline) with paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed=1729) and performed an exact McNemar two‑sided test for discordant pairs. Missingness policy (complete‑pair primary) and sensitivity analyses were preregistered; execution produced complete pairs for all planned units.

sections.discussion:
Interpretation and causal explanation: The preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics produced exactly one generated candidate per pair that both baseline and guarded conditions consumed. In this run, that single shared candidate passed the deterministic oracle for all 200 pairs, which prevented the repair stage from ever being invoked (repair_calls_invoked=0). Consequently, both conditions consumed identical passing artifacts and the paired difference is degenerate (0.00). The measured null effect therefore reflects the preregistered design and observed generator behavior, not a general refutation of verifier‑assisted repair in settings where initial candidates sometimes fail.

Methodological lessons and operational implications: (1) generation semantics matter: shared_initial_candidate measures a different estimand (the effect of downstream verification/repair when generator variance is turned off) than an independent‑generation design that would allow repairs to act on different candidate draws per condition. (2) task difficulty calibration is essential: if the generator routinely produces passing candidates for the chosen task bank and model, repairs will not be exercised and the confirmatory test cannot measure repair benefit. (3) artifact‑anchored reproducibility: because every prompt, output, provider trace and validator trace is archived and SHA‑256 hashed, researchers can deterministically replay or extend the run under alternate preregistered generation semantics or task banks while preserving auditability.

Recommendations (artifact‑grounded follow‑ups): Using only archived artifacts and without inventing new data, two immediate preregistered variants would permit informative measurement of repair benefit: (A) independent generation semantics: change generation_semantics to independent_per_condition (one generator call per condition per pair), rerun with identical task manifest seeds; expected model_calls_used ≈ 400 and the repair budget can then be expended when baseline candidates fail; (B) calibrated harder tasks: augment execution/task_manifest.jsonl with higher‑difficulty tasks or boundary cases (the manifest format and generator seeds are archived), then rerun under either shared_initial_candidate or independent generation to provoke oracle failures. Other reproducible variants include increasing the repair budget (>1), enabling iterative repair loops, or repeating the experiment with additional models. All of these variants are executable using the same adapter family and the archived prompt and task manifests; the execution framework will produce new per‑file SHA‑256 digests for deterministic reconciliation.

Threats to validity (artifact‑grounded): Internal validity — the single most important internal threat is the preregistered generation semantics (shared_initial_candidate) which produced the ceiling effect. Construct validity — the deterministic validator assesses operationally meaningful predicates (required sequence, protected interfaces, reachability) but may miss nuanced real‑device idiosyncrasies; validator coverage diagnostics are available per pair. External validity — single declared model (gpt‑5‑mini), synthetic/emulated tasks and deterministic emulation limit generalization to production heterogeneous images and other models. Conclusion validity — inference is exact for the frozen estimand and observed data; however the degenerate contingency (no discordant pairs) means the confirmatory test cannot speak to repair efficacy in regimes where initial candidates fail.

What this null does and does not show: It shows that, under the specific preregistered design (shared_initial_candidate, gpt‑5‑mini, chosen task bank and deterministic validator), a verifier‑assisted repair module had zero opportunity to act and therefore produced no measurable benefit. It does not show that verifier‑assisted repair cannot reduce misconfiguration in other plausible designs where generator variability and task difficulty create initial failures.
sections.conclusion: We preregistered and executed an auditable paired emulation test of verifier‑assisted generate→validate→repair under shared_initial_candidate generation semantics. Both baseline and guarded conditions achieved 200/200 oracle passes; repairs were never invoked; paired difference=0.00 (95% bootstrap CI [0.00,0.00]; McNemar p=1.00). The null outcome is explained by the preregistered generation semantics and corresponding ceiling effect. The primary scientific lesson is methodological: to measure the operational benefit of verifier‑assisted repair, experimenters must (a) permit independent generator variance per condition or (b) calibrate task difficulty so that initial candidates sometimes fail. We publish the full hashed artifact bundle (preregistration, master prompt provenance, raw outputs, provider traces, validator traces, execution manifest and analysis artifacts) so that future runs implementing those recommended variants can be executed and deterministically audited.

limitations: Confirmatory conclusions apply only to the exact preregistered design (shared_initial_candidate semantics, gpt‑5‑mini, deterministic_netops_validator_v5, and the provided synthetic/emulated 200‑pair task bank).

Shared_initial_candidate semantics created a ceiling effect: because the single shared generated candidate per pair passed the deterministic oracle for every task, the repair stage was never invoked (repair_calls_invoked = 0), preventing measurable guarded benefit in this run.
Emulation with a deterministic validator and synthetic tasks does not capture full production heterogeneity (real vendor images, runtime nondeterminism, device‑specific quirks).
Single‑model execution limits generality across model families and instruction‑tuning variants; additional models and independent generation semantics are needed to measure cross‑model robustness.
Repair budget was intentionally limited (≤1 call/task) by preregistration; richer iterative repair policies remain unexplored in this run.
Oracle blind spots (uncovered semantic failure modes) remain possible; per‑pair oracle_coverage diagnostics are archived and should be consulted when extending the study.
